storm.summary_layperson: Strong thunderstorm cells are bearing down from the west-northwest and expected at the cove around 5:15–5:50 PM; Long Island Sound provides only weak protection today, so this storm should be treated as a real threat.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water at 74.5°F is only 6°F cooler than the air — a weak marine layer that may take a modest edge off incoming storms as they cross the water, but not enough to stop them.
storm.detail_html:
Three radar-tracked cells are closing on Greenwich Cove from the WNW. The lead cell is 27 miles out at 46 dBZ, moving southeast at 20 knots; a stronger 55 dBZ cell follows a half-mile behind it. Storm motion is measured from two radar scans 22 minutes apart — the track is reliable. Arrival is expected around 5:32 PM, with the window running 5:15–5:50 PM for the lead cell. A slower third cell (36 dBZ, approaching from due W) trails and may arrive around 6:10 PM (window 5:43–6:37 PM).

The regional environment supports active convection. CAPE is 1,700 J/kg and the NWS Area Forecast Discussion flags scattered showers and thunderstorms this afternoon into early evening with the potential for isolated severe gusts and small hail. A Flood Watch is in effect through Wednesday morning, driven primarily by heavy rainfall expected Tuesday, but the immediate afternoon convective threat is today's concern.

Long Island Sound's protective effect is weak today. Sound water is 74.5°F against 80.6°F inland air — only a 6°F differential. Cells approaching perpendicular from the WNW will cross the Sound before reaching the cove, which gives the stable layer a chance to choke some low-level fuel. The pipeline rates this a moderate Sound effect, meaning the cove may see slightly less intense rain and thunder than areas two miles inland. However, formal strong protection requires a water–air gap above 10°F; today's 6°F falls well short. The storm will arrive; the Sound may file the sharp edges off it, not stop it.

The most likely outcome is a significant squall around 5:15–5:50 PM: gusty winds (likely 20–30+ knots during the peak squall passage, not captured in the hourly HRRR model values), heavy rain, lightning, and thunder. After the storm clears — probably by 18:00–18:30 — a steady S–SW gradient wind at 9–11 knots should re-establish through the rest of the evening.

What would change the call: if upstream APRS stations to the WNW (Rye, Port Chester) begin spiking gusts before 5:15 PM, the gust front is outrunning the radar echo and arrival will beat the prediction. If the cells reorganize or slow over the Sound, arrival shifts toward the late edge (5:50 PM) with reduced intensity. The 55 dBZ cell just behind the lead is the one to watch — if the two cells merge, intensity and duration could exceed the point estimate.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cells 27 miles WNW closing at 20 knots; the Sound's weak marine layer may shave a few minutes off the late edge, but the arrival window should be taken at face value.

wind.regime_label: Moderate gradient wind — sea breeze not established

hourly.shift_note: veering SW through sunset, peak of evening

wind.tactics_blurb: If the storm clears by 18:00–18:30, a S–SW gradient at 9–11 knots makes the post-storm period raceable with relatively even pressure across the cove; start mid-line and favor right on the first beat as the wind briefly veers SW near sunset.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a moderate gradient wind day — the evening S/SE/SW flow is driven by the large-scale pressure pattern, not a sea-breeze thermal. The two-ingredient sea-breeze check falls short: the air–water temperature difference (6.1°F) barely clears the 5°F minimum, but only 48% of coastal stations are showing southerly flow — well below the 60% threshold for an established sea breeze — and both the CT coast and LI north shore subregion fractions are weak (30% and 20% respectively). The authoritative anemometer average is 8.3 knots, squarely in the moderate-gradient range. Because this is not a sea-breeze day, the sea-breeze direction maturation correction does not apply; the HRRR hourly directions are used as-is for the forecast table.

The central tactical fact for this window is the storm arriving around 5:15–5:50 PM EDT — at the very opening of the racing period. Expect racing to be under AP or postponed when the cells arrive. During squall passage, winds will spike well above the HRRR hourly values; the model's hourly time steps do not resolve the squall-line peak. Plan on 15–30+ knot gusts during cell passage, followed by a lull (HRRR shows 5 kt SSE at 18:00, consistent with the post-squall calm). Note that there is a large HRRR/obs divergence right now — HRRR's f01 direction is E at 92°, while stations are already showing S/SE at 134–175° — but on a gradient day this reflects synoptic flow rather than a sea-breeze lag, and the HRRR f02–f06 hourly progression is the right forecast to use.

Post-storm (18:00 onward), a S–SW gradient at 9–11 knots is expected to establish and hold through most of the evening. HRRR shows the wind building from SSE 5 kt at 18:00 → S 9 kt at 19:00 → SW 11 kt at 20:00 (near sunset) → backing to S 9 kt at 21:00, then fading toward 4 kt by 22:00. CAPE collapses from 1,460 J/kg at 19:00 to 610 J/kg at 20:00 — consistent with the storm flushing the atmospheric instability — so the post-storm gradient is drier and stabler, less prone to further convective disruption.

With post-storm direction in the S–SSW range, flow enters the cove along its primary north–south axis — the cleanest, most consistent orientation for the race area. Pressure should be relatively even across the course. As direction momentarily veers to SW around 20:00 (near sunset at ~20:10), the right side of the beat gains a small lift advantage; that advantage fades as the wind backs to S again after dark. Because this is a gradient day, there is no thermal collapse — the wind fades gradually through the evening rather than dropping off a cliff at sunset.

For fleet racing: 9–11 kt S/SW is solid dinghy wind — the sweet spot for one-design classes. If the storm clears cleanly by 18:00–18:30, there is roughly a 2.5-hour window of good breeze before the wind fades past 5 kt near 22:00. The main risks are the storm lingering past 18:00 (which would eliminate the evening window) and direction instability in the first 10–15 minutes after storm passage while the gradient resets. Recommend waiting for RYC to show consistent S at 7+ knots for a 10-minute average before starting.
